thread.title: Papa John’s and 3 Other Small-Cap Value Plays

author: Jack Hough
title: Papa John’s and 3 Other Small-Cap Value Plays
text:
Illustration: Luke Sharrett/Bloomberg via Getty Images By Jack Hough Aug. 7, 2018 1:27 p.m. ET Stocks that are sparsely covered by Wall Street analysts deserve some added attention from investors, according to new research from investment bank Jefferies. Below are four names Barron’s culled from a recent screen by the firm.
Large companies tend to be covered by more analysts than smaller ones, but size isn’t a perfect predictor of coverage. The second-largest U.S. company by market value, Amazon.com (ticker: AMZN), has 49 analysts contributing earnings estimates for its current fiscal year, five more than the largest company, Apple (AAPL), according to FactSet. Retailer J.C. Penney (JCP), worth less than $1 billion, has 16 analysts, the same as $240 billion drugmaker Pfizer (PFE).
Newsletter Sign-up The number of analysts covering a company is, of course, not the most important predictor of stock performance, but it might have some predictive ability, at least among smaller companies. For companies in the Russell 2000 index, where the average market value is just over $2 billion, those with coverage by 10 or more analysts tend to underperform the index by 2.7 percentage points a year, while those covered by three to 10 analysts tend to outperform by a percentage point, according to a recent analysis by Jefferies.
The latter group, then, might be a good place to begin a search for value. Jefferies has Buy ratings on 35 companies covered by three to 10 analysts, and 11 of them are on its Focus List. Among these, the following four have price targets that are more than 35% above their recent share prices.
Papa John’s International (PZZA)
Jefferies target price: $58
Upside from recent price: 37%
Shares of Papa John’s have tumbled 46% in a year amid founder John Schnatter leaving the company over remarks that sparked a customer backlash . Schnatter stepped down as chief executive last December and chairman last month. Papa John’s trades now at 20 times this year’s earnings forecast, but sales and earnings have both taken a hit this year. Jefferies analyst Alex Slagle recently upgraded the stock, citing potential for a business rebound or a takeover. Based on 2020 estimates, shares trade at 14 times earnings.
Karyopharm Therapeutics (KPTI)
Target price: $27
Upside from recent price: 49%
Karyopharm is a development-stage drug company testing a treatment for multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that is one of the diseases targeted by Celgene ’s (CELG) $9 billion drug Revlimid. If Karyopharm’s drug, Selinexor, can gain accelerated approval for patients who have gone through most other treatments, it could come to market next year, with longer-term potential for expanded use. The risk and opportunity for investors in Karyopharm, valued at just over $1 billion, is illustrated by Wall Street’s long-term financial projections: Among three analysts who have ventured to predict 2022 revenues, the lowest says $305 million, and the highest, $2.5 billion.
OptiNose (OPTN)
Target price: $32
Upside from recent price: 42%
OptiNose has a drug called Xhance for chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) with polyps, and is being tested for CRS without polyps. CRS is characterized by nasal blockage. What is unique about OptiNose’s treatment is the delivery system, which looks like an inhaler but is better described as an exhaler, where breath from the patient’s mouth propels medicine up into one nostril. The idea is to reach parts of the nasal passages that traditional nasal sprays don’t get to. Valued at just under $900 million, OptiNose currently loses money, but if long-term projections are reliable, it could turn a $100 million profit by 2022.
Arris International (ARRS)
Target price: $38
Upside from recent price: 57%
Arris trades at eight times this year’s projected earnings, a level that implies a potential for declines. Yet Wall Street predicts modest revenue growth and gains of 7% to 12% a year in earnings per share over the next three years. Investors are likely turned off by the company’s exposure to set-top boxes at a time when cable subscriptions are at risk of long-term customer defections to streaming services. Arris is adding features to set-top boxes like voice control, wireless connections, and the ability to stream to tablets and phones to help cable companies stay competitive, but it has the option of selling the division down the road. Networking and cloud operations bring in about two-thirds of company earnings.
